findings.reason: as written, one of the plan's three consumers (§8) cannot execute in the state the plan defines, and a manual dispatch is disabled by a setting that is not about it; the author must decide whether the setting is a property of the plan or only of the service and say so in §4's reason list.
findings.text: §4 lists "its project has switched service queueing off" as one of the fixed reasons a plan may not be queued and says "the whole-plan dispatch refuses … by that same answer", while §7 describes that setting as switching off the *service* and §8 says it queues an idle wait's upstream "whatever the project's service setting" — under the setting off, §4 must answer "may not", so §8's precondition fails and its arm is unreachable, and a coordinator's own whole-plan dispatch is refused by a setting meant to govern the automated service

findings.reason: the plan asserts an existing mechanism performs a job it cannot, so §7 as built would let the service queue a plan a coordinator believes it has held; either a plan-level hold must be named as something this section adds, or the exemption must be restated.
findings.text: §7 says "a coordinator keeps a plan out of it with the queue hold that already exists", but `crew queue hold --plan` selects only *already filed* waiting requests (`reckon/crew/queue_edit.py:1003` → `_selected_requests`, which raises "no waiting requests found for …" when the plan has none) and writes each pointer in place; a plan with no request cannot be held, and requests the service files afterwards are not covered

findings.reason: splitting the obligation out (or dropping it to a consumer of the read) lets each deliverable be dispatched, gated and reviewed on one measure.
findings.text: §4 delivers both the single per-plan queueability read (with its fixed reason list and its two dispatch call-sites) and a new obligation kind on a session, and its own title names the two, so one gate has to prove a read function and an obligation surface and a reviewer cannot close the section on one verdict

findings.reason: the counting rule has no defined answer for the population the lane document actually counts, so the implementer would have to invent one; the plan should scope the count to upstream waits or name what an unclassified request counts as.
findings.text: §6 opens "The admit pass already stamps every waiting request with a class", but every write of `wait_class` lives in the upstream-resolution path of `reckon/crew/admission/release.py` (lines 270, 655, 684, 692, 752, 799), so a request waiting for a lane slot carries no class; §6 then requires the lane document — whose `waiting` figure is the gate's queued population — to give its count by the recorded class while forbidding it from recomputing one, leaving no value for the unclassified requests

response_events.note: the project switch is no longer one of section 4's reasons; it is section 7's own setting, and section 8 says it applies whatever that setting is
section 7 now extends the existing queue hold command to accept a plan with no request yet and to cover requests filed later, and names that as an added form
section 4 is now the read alone; the obligation is the new section 10 with its own gate
section 6 now says only upstream waits carry a class, counts slot waits as their own part, and is limited to the queue view; the lane document is left alone
